title: Coxeter Polyhedral Gluings and Intrinsic Metrics

items.title: Abstract isometric polyhedral gluings and the chain metric
items.statement:
**Shape and face posets.** Let $(P,\le)$ be a poset ([[def-partial-order]]) with least element $\varnothing$ such that:

(a) for every $p\in P$ the principal down-set $P_{\le p}:=\{r\in P:r\le p\}$ is finite and, when $p\ne\varnothing$, is isomorphic as a poset to the face poset of a nonempty compact convex polyhedral cell ([[def-finite-convex-cell-complex-and-linear-subdivision]], [[def-face-poset-and-order-complex]]);

(b) every two elements $p,q\in P$ have a greatest lower bound $p\wedge q$ in $P$, that is, an element of $P$ that is a lower bound of both and is larger than every such lower bound.

The elements of $P$ are called **faces**, $p\le q$ is read "$p$ is a face of $q$", and $\varnothing$ is the **empty face**.

**Isometric polyhedral gluing.** An *isometric polyhedral gluing of shape $P$* consists of the following data.

**(i) Cells and face isometries.** For every $p\in P\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ a nonempty compact convex polyhedral cell $C_p$ in a finite-dimensional Euclidean affine space, and for every pair $p\le q$ of nonempty faces a nonempty face $F_{p,q}$ of $C_q$ together with an affine isometry $h_{p,q}$ from the affine span of $C_p$ onto the affine span of $F_{p,q}$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]) which carries $C_p$ onto $F_{p,q}$, subject to:

- $h_{p,p}=\operatorname{id}_{C_p}$ for every $p$;
- the *cocycle condition* $h_{q,r}\circ h_{p,q}=h_{p,r}$ whenever $p\le q\le r$;
- for every $q$ the assignment $p\mapsto F_{p,q}=h_{p,q}(C_p)$ is an isomorphism of posets from $P_{\le q}\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ onto the set of nonempty faces of $C_q$, ordered by inclusion.

**(ii) Quotient and intersection condition.** Let $X$ be the quotient of the disjoint union $\bigsqcup_{p\in P\setminus\{\varnothing\}}C_p$ by the equivalence relation generated by $x\sim h_{p,q}(x)$ for $x\in C_p$ and $p\le q$, and let $\iota_p\colon C_p\to X$ denote the quotient map. The *intersection condition* is:

- each $\iota_p$ is injective; and
- for all nonempty faces $p,q$ one has $\iota_p(C_p)\cap\iota_q(C_q)=\iota_{p\wedge q}(C_{p\wedge q})$, where the right-hand side denotes the empty subset of $X$ when $p\wedge q=\varnothing$.

**(iii) Weak topology.** A subset $U\subseteq X$ is declared open if and only if $U\cap\iota_p(C_p)$ is relatively open in $\iota_p(C_p)$ for every nonempty face $p$ ([[def-metric-topology]]).

**Standing hypotheses.** (H1) *Connectedness*: $X\ne\emptyset$ and $X$ is connected. (H2) *Local finiteness*: every point of $X$ lies in $\iota_p(C_p)$ for only finitely many $p$. (H3) *Finite shapes*: the cells $C_p$ fall into only finitely many isometry classes. By (H1) at least one cell exists, so by (H3) the maximum $D:=\max\{\dim C_p:p\in P\setminus\{\varnothing\}\}$ of the dimensions of the cells is a well-defined natural number.

**Chains and the chain metric candidate.** Write $d_p$ for the Euclidean metric on the affine span of $C_p$. Let $x,y\in X$. A **chain** from $x$ to $y$ is a finite sequence $x=x_0,x_1,\dots,x_m=y$ of points of $X$ such that for each $i\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ some cell contains both $x_{i-1}$ and $x_i$; for $m=0$ the chain is the one-term sequence $x$. Its **length** is
$$\ell(x_0,\dots,x_m):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}d_{p_i}(x_{i-1},x_i),$$
where for each $i$ the face $p_i$ is *any* nonempty face with $x_{i-1},x_i\in\iota_{p_i}(C_{p_i})$; this number does not depend on these choices. The **chain metric candidate** of the gluing is
$$d(x,y):=\inf\bigl\{\,\ell(x_0,\dots,x_m):x_0,\dots,x_m\text{ is a chain from }x\text{ to }y\,\bigr\}.$$
Because $X$ is connected, every two points of $X$ are joined by a chain (this and the independence of $\ell$ from the chosen faces are proved in [[thm-cg-polyhedral-chain-metric-topology-and-properness]]), so the infimum is taken over a nonempty set of real numbers, and $0\le d(x,y)<\infty$. This finiteness follows from (H1) and the gluing data; it is not an additional hypothesis.

**What is asserted, and what is not.** For all $x,y,z\in X$ one has $d(x,x)=0$ (the one-term chain), $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$ (reverse a chain) and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$ (concatenate chains), and these three facts need no hypothesis beyond the definitions. No other metric axiom, no agreement of $d$ with the weak topology, and no completeness, properness or geodesic property is asserted here: those are the conclusions of the theorems of this page, under (H1)–(H3).

**Caveat on cell metrics.** If $x,y$ lie in a common cell then the one-step chain gives $d(x,y)\le d_p(x,y)$, but equality can fail, because a chain may leave the cell and return with smaller total length (Bridson–Haefliger I.7.6). Nothing above asserts that the chain metric restricts to the Euclidean metric of a cell, and no cell is assumed to be geodesic for $d$.
items.strategy: The definition is a conditional construction, so its well-definedness obligations are (a) that the length of a chain is independent of the choice of common cells, and (b) that $d$ is finite-valued under (H1). For (a), two cells containing both $x_{i-1}$ and $x_i$ meet in a common face containing both points, and the Euclidean distances computed in the two cells agree because the straight segment between the points lies in that face. For (b), fix $x$ and let $A$ be the set of points joined to $x$ by a chain; a cell meeting $A$ in one point is contained in $A$ (append a one-step chain), so $A\cap C_p$ is either $C_p$ or empty for every cell $p$, whence $A$ is clopen in the weak topology; connectedness of $X$ gives $A=X$, so the infimum defining $d(x,y)$ is over a nonempty set. The metric axioms beyond symmetry and the triangle inequality are deliberately not part of the definition: nondegeneracy, the topology comparison and completeness are proved in [[thm-cg-polyhedral-chain-metric-topology-and-properness]], which is the justification target of this definition. The finite-shapes and local-finiteness hypotheses are declared before any metric claim, and no equality of $d$ with a cellwise Euclidean metric is assumed (Bridson-Haefliger I.7.6).

items.title: Face coherence, global hat coordinates and a uniform star radius
items.statement:
Let $X$ be an isometric polyhedral gluing with standing hypotheses (H1)-(H3) of [[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]], with chain metric candidate $d$, maximal dimension $D$ and finite model list. Write $P^{*}:=P\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ and let $K$ be the order complex ([[def-face-poset-and-order-complex]]) of $P^{*}$: its vertices are the elements of $P^{*}$ and its simplices are the finite chains in $P^{*}$.

For every $p\in P^{*}$ let $b_p$ be the **barycentre** of $C_p$, that is, the average of its vertices, the vertices of a compact convex polyhedral cell being its $0$-dimensional faces. Then:

**(i) Compatible barycentric triangulation.** Each $b_p$ is a point of the relative interior of $C_p$. The canonical map $\Phi\colon|K|\to X$ that sends a vertex $p$ to $b_p$ and a simplex, that is a chain $F_0<\dots<F_k$ in $P^{*}$, affinely onto the convex hull of $b_{F_0},\dots,b_{F_k}$ inside $C_{F_k}$ is well defined, is a bijection onto $X$, and is a homeomorphism from the weak topology of $|K|$ to the weak topology of $X$. Consequently every point of $X$ lies in the relative interior of exactly one of these simplices, its **carrier simplex**, whose dimension is at most $D$.

**(ii) Hat coordinates and a uniform Lipschitz constant.** For every vertex $v\in P^{*}$ let $\lambda_v\colon X\to[0,1]$ assign to $x$ the barycentric coordinate of its carrier simplex at $v$; equivalently $\lambda_v(\Phi(\alpha))=\alpha(v)$ for $\alpha\in|K|$ ([[def-geometric-realization-of-an-abstract-simplicial-complex]]). Then each $\lambda_v$ is well defined, $\sum_{v}\lambda_v(x)=1$ for every $x\in X$ with only finitely many nonzero terms, each $\lambda_v$ is affine on every simplex of $K$, and there is a real constant $L<\infty$, depending only on the finite model list, with
$$|\lambda_v(x)-\lambda_v(y)|\le L\,d(x,y)$$
for all $x,y\in X$ and every $v$. Explicitly, one may take for $L$ the maximum of $1$ and of the finitely many slopes $1/h$ of the barycentric coordinate at a vertex of a positive-dimensional simplex of the barycentric subdivision of a model cell, where $h>0$ is the distance from that vertex to the affine hull of the opposite face of that simplex.

Coordinates on singleton simplices are constant and contribute slope $0$; if every cell is a point, take $L=1$.

**(iii) Uniform star radius and finite stars.** For every $x\in X$ there is a vertex $v$ with $\lambda_v(x)\ge1/(D+1)$; for such a $v$ the open ball $B(x,\delta)$ of radius $\delta:=1/(2L(D+1))$ is contained in the open star of $v$ ([[def-simplicial-subcomplex-star-closure-and-link]]), transported to $X$ along $\Phi$. Every closed star is the image under $\Phi$ of the realization of a finite subcomplex of $K$, and it is compact and metrizable in the weak topology; the open stars cover $X$; and for every vertex $v$ only finitely many vertices lie with $v$ in a common cell.
items.strategy: Use compact extrema to find vertices in each face and prove that their average is relatively interior. Cone face triangulations from those canonical barycentres; affine face isometries preserve them and the intersection condition gives unique carriers. The finite weak-topology supplier gives the barycentric homeomorphism. Bound coordinate slopes by reciprocal opposite-face heights only on positive-dimensional model simplices; singleton slopes are zero, and take L>=1. Subdivide cell segments, sum the slope bound along chains, then take the infimum. A carrier has at most D+1 vertices, so one coordinate is >=1/(D+1), giving delta=1/(2L(D+1)). H2 gives finitely many cofaces at a barycentre and finite downsets give finite closed stars and adjacency. D=0 uses L=1.

items.title: The chain metric is a metric, its topology is the weak topology, and the space is proper and complete
items.statement:
Let $X$ be an isometric polyhedral gluing with standing hypotheses (H1)-(H3) of [[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]], let $d$ be its chain metric candidate, and let $L$ and $\delta$ be the constants of [[lem-cg-polyhedral-face-coherence-and-uniform-star-radius]] for this gluing. Then:

**(1) Well-definedness and metric.** The length of a chain does not depend on the cells chosen to measure its steps, every two points of $X$ are joined by a chain, and $d\colon X\times X\to[0,\infty)$ is a metric on $X$: for all $x,y,z\in X$, $d(x,x)=0$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, $d(x,y)>0$ whenever $x\ne y$, and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$ ([[def-metric-space]]).

**(2) Topology.** The metric topology of $d$ ([[def-metric-topology]]) coincides with the weak topology of the gluing: a subset of $X$ is open in the metric topology if and only if its trace on every closed cell is relatively open.

**(3) Properness and completeness.** Every closed $d$-bounded subset of $X$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]); in particular $(X,d)$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]) and every closed ball is compact. No bound on the number of cells meeting a vertex is needed beyond local finiteness.
items.strategy: Common meet faces make chain lengths independent; clopen reachability gives finite-valued chains from H1. Equal hat coordinates separate points. Traverse a positive-length chain in cell segments and sample at gaps delta/2; meeting open stars have vertices in a common cell. The locally finite adjacency graph therefore gives a finite closed-star cover of each bounded ball. Distance functions restricted to a cell are Euclidean 1-Lipschitz, so metric-open sets are weakly open. Transfer the weak compactness of each finite star to its metric subspace by open covers; finite unions and closed-subset compactness prove properness. The compact-metric continuous-bijection theorem on a finite realization gives the reverse topology inclusion inside a star. A Cauchy sequence lies in a positive-radius compact complete ball. Include the starting-point branch for zero chains and the empty closed subset.

items.title: Length in a metric target: lower semicontinuity and arc-length reparametrization
items.statement:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $a<b$ be real numbers. A **path** in $X$ is a map $\gamma\colon[a,b]\to X$. A **partition** of $[a,b]$ is a finite sequence $a=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_m=b$; the **polygonal sum** of $\gamma$ over that partition is $\sum_{i=1}^{m}d(\gamma(t_{i-1}),\gamma(t_i))$, and the **length** of $\gamma$ is the supremum
$$L(\gamma):=\sup\Bigl\{\,\sum_{i=1}^{m}d(\gamma(t_{i-1}),\gamma(t_i)) : a=t_0<\dots<t_m=b\,\Bigr\}\in[0,\infty]$$
For a singleton interval $[u,u]$, its only partition is the one-term sequence $u$, its polygonal sum is the empty sum $0$, and its path length is $0$. For nondegenerate intervals the supremum is taken in the extended reals ([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]], [[def-upper-bound]]); $\gamma$ is **rectifiable** if $L(\gamma)<\infty$. For $[u,v]\subseteq[a,b]$ write $\gamma|_{[u,v]}$ for the restriction of $\gamma$ to $[u,v]$, a path on $[u,v]$, and $L(\gamma|_{[u,v]})$ for its length.

**Chord bound and additivity at the initial point.** For $a\le u\le v\le b$ one has $d(\gamma(u),\gamma(v))\le L(\gamma|_{[u,v]})$, and for $a\le v\le w\le b$ one has $L(\gamma|_{[a,w]})=L(\gamma|_{[a,v]})+L(\gamma|_{[v,w]})$; in particular $s(t):=L(\gamma|_{[a,t]})$ is nondecreasing on $[a,b]$.

**(i) Lower semicontinuity.** If $\gamma_k,\gamma\colon[a,b]\to X$ are paths with $\sup_{t\in[a,b]}d(\gamma_k(t),\gamma(t))\to0$ (uniform convergence, [[def-topology-of-uniform-convergence]]), then $L(\gamma)\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}L(\gamma_k)$, the limit inferior being taken in $[0,\infty]$ ([[def-limsup-and-liminf-of-nonnegative-extended-sequences]]).

**(ii) Arc-length parametrization.** If $\gamma$ is continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]) and rectifiable, with $L:=L(\gamma)<\infty$, then $s(t):=L(\gamma|_{[a,t]})$ defines a continuous nondecreasing surjection $s\colon[a,b]\to[0,L]$ with $s(a)=0$ and $s(b)=L$; there is a unique map $\bar\gamma\colon[0,L]\to X$ with $\gamma=\bar\gamma\circ s$; and $\bar\gamma$ is $1$-Lipschitz with $L(\bar\gamma|_{[r,q]})=q-r$ for all $0\le r\le q\le L$. If $L=0$ then $\gamma$ is constant, $[0,L]=\{0\}$, and $\bar\gamma$ is that constant.

**(iii) Equicontinuity of bounded arc-length families.** Call a path $\gamma\colon[a,b]\to X$ **arc-length parametrized** when $L(\gamma)<\infty$ and
$$L(\gamma|_{[s,t]})=\frac{t-s}{b-a}\,L(\gamma)\qquad\text{for all } a\le s\le t\le b .$$
If $M<\infty$ and the paths $\gamma_k\colon[0,1]\to X$ are arc-length parametrized with $L(\gamma_k)\le M$ for every $k$, then each $\gamma_k$ is $M$-Lipschitz and the family $(\gamma_k)$ is equicontinuous and uniformly equicontinuous ([[def-equicontinuity]]).

**(iv) Application to polyhedral gluings.** If $X$ carries the chain metric $d$ of an isometric polyhedral gluing with hypotheses (H1)-(H3) ([[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]]), then $d$ is a metric on $X$ ([[thm-cg-polyhedral-chain-metric-topology-and-properness]] (1)), and clauses (i)-(iii) apply verbatim to paths in $(X,d)$.

No compactness, completeness, convexity or local structure of $X$ is used in (i)-(iii), and no Euclidean-target theorem on arc length is invoked: the statements are proved in the stated metric generality.
items.strategy: Use the one-term partition of length zero on singleton intervals. Partition refinement and concatenation give the chord bound and additivity, including infinite length. Uniform convergence gives convergence of each fixed finite polygonal sum; a strict gap contradicts any proposed upper bound of all tail infima. For a continuous rectifiable path, a near-maximal partition and the reverse triangle inequality bound nearby restriction lengths and give continuous arclength s. IVT gives surjectivity and zero-length fibres give the unique factorization. The chord bound gives a 1-Lipschitz reparametrization. Canonical supremum preimages transfer partitions back and forth, giving the reverse length inequality and exact unit speed; treat r=q by the singleton convention first. This construction requires no Choice. Bounded normalized families are M-Lipschitz, with M=0 treated separately.

items.title: Under the Axiom of Choice, proper polyhedral spaces admit minimizing geodesics
items.statement: **Assume the Axiom of Choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be an isometric polyhedral gluing with standing hypotheses (H1)-(H3) of [[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]], so that $(X,d)$ is a proper metric space by [[thm-cg-polyhedral-chain-metric-topology-and-properness]]. Then every pair $x,y\in X$ is joined by a minimizing geodesic: there is a path $\gamma\colon[0,d(x,y)]\to X$ with $\gamma(0)=x$, $\gamma(d(x,y))=y$ and $d(\gamma(s),\gamma(t))=|s-t|$ for all $s,t$ ([[def-geodesic-and-geodesic-metric-space]]); in particular $(X,d)$ is a geodesic metric space. More precisely, every sequence of chains from $x$ to $y$ whose lengths tend to $d(x,y)$ has a subsequence whose associated polygonal paths, each traversed at constant speed on the common domain $[0,1]$, converge uniformly to a continuous path of length $d(x,y)$ whose arc-length reparametrization is a minimizing geodesic from $x$ to $y$. The case $x=y$ is included: then $d(x,y)=0$ and the degenerate interval $[0,0]=\{0\}$ carries the geodesic $\gamma(0)=x$.
items.strategy: Assume AC explicitly. Straight cell segments traversed at constant Euclidean speed give ell-Lipschitz paths of metric length at most chain length; cell shortcuts prevent assuming equality. AC selects countably many near-minimizing chains and their finite common-cell witnesses. These paths are equicontinuous and pointwise bounded, and AC-dependent Ascoli on the nonempty compact domain [0,1] with the proper target gives a uniform subsequence. Every tail infimum is <=R+epsilon for every epsilon>0; lower semicontinuity and the endpoint chord bound force length R. Arc-length parametrization and the endpoint triangle force equality of each chord with parameter difference. For any prescribed length-convergent chain sequence, select realizing witnesses if needed and use M=1+sup ell_n>0 for the common Lipschitz and containing-ball bounds. Zero chains give constant paths and the geodesic on [0,0].

items.strategy: Induct on the number of edges, cut a leaf interval, remove chain excursions at its attaching endpoint, and prove the recursive chain-distance formula before using it. Prove geodesic existence by concatenating the interval segment with the smaller-tree geodesic, and uniqueness by injectivity of distance from x on the metric interval I(x,y). Apply the weighted formula to vertices, midpoints and the comparison with the discrete graph metric.

items.title: A locally finite shrinking-edge ray is not complete
items.strategy: Define the gluing explicitly and check the axioms. (iii): identify each point of $X$ with the arclength coordinate of its location along the ray; the chain metric coincides with the Euclidean metric on $[0,2)$ because a chain cannot be shortened below the absolute difference of coordinates (triangle inequality on the line) and the direct segments realize it. (iv): the vertex distances are $d(p_k,p_m)=s_m-s_k$ for $m>k$, so $(p_k)$ is Cauchy; if it converged to $p\in C_N$, then $p$ has coordinate at most $s_N=2-2^{-N}$ while $p_k$ has coordinate $s_k=2-2^{-k}$, so $d(p,p_k)\ge s_k-s_N=2^{-N}-2^{-k}\ge 2^{-(N+1)}$ for every $k>N$, contradicting $d(p,p_k)\to0$. Equivalently, $[0,2)$ is not complete, and a Cauchy sequence without limit exists. (v): two intervals $C_n$, $C_m$ are isometric only if $n=m$, so infinitely many isometry classes occur although the gluing is locally finite; the closed ball of radius $2$ is the whole non-compact space, so properness also fails. This is the phenomenon behind Bridson-Haefliger I.7.11 and the design's warning.

items.title: The hexagonal $A_2$ cell: Euclidean cell metric versus graph distance
items.statement:
Let $H\subset\mathbb R^2$ be the regular hexagon of side length $1$ with vertices $v_0,\dots,v_5$ in cyclic order, regarded as a single compact convex $2$-cell of an isometric polyhedral gluing, with one maximal cell, its six sides and its six vertices (three shapes). This is the $A_2$ Coxeter cell for an equidistant generic point: step 3.1 verifies the reflection presentation $\langle s,t\mid s^2=t^2=(st)^3=1\rangle$, computes its six-point orbit, and identifies $H$ with the orbit hull (Davis, Definition 7.3.1 and Examples 7.3.2(ii)). Explicitly, take
$$H:=\{(x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb R^2:\ |x_2|\le\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\ |\sqrt3x_1+x_2|\le\sqrt3,\ |\sqrt3x_1-x_2|\le\sqrt3\}$$
and let
$$v_0=(1,0),\ v_1=(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}),\ v_2=(-\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}),\ v_3=(-1,0),\ v_4=(-\tfrac12,-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}),\ v_5=(\tfrac12,-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2});$$
the inequalities written out are the six affine inequalities $\pm x_2\le\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $\pm(\sqrt3x_1+x_2)\le\sqrt3$, $\pm(\sqrt3x_1-x_2)\le\sqrt3$. They also give $|x_1|\le1$, since $2\sqrt3|x_1|\le|\sqrt3x_1+x_2|+|\sqrt3x_1-x_2|\le2\sqrt3$. Thus $H$ is nonempty (it contains $0$), bounded and defined by finitely many closed affine inequalities, hence is a compact convex polyhedral cell; the verification below identifies its vertices and sides. Let $d$ be the chain metric of the gluing. Then:

**(i)** for a single convex cell the chain metric is the Euclidean metric: $d(x,y)=|x-y|_2$ for all $x,y\in H$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]);

**(ii)** $(H,d)$ is a complete geodesic space; the straight segment $[x,y]\subseteq H$ realizes $d$, by completeness and convexity of $H$ as verified here;

**(iii)** the barycentric triangulation of $H$ (the order complex of the face poset of the single cell) has vertices the six polygon vertices, the six edge midpoints and the centre $o$, and twelve congruent right triangles $v\,m\,o$, one for every incident vertex-edge pair $v<e$ with midpoint $m$; each has legs $|vm|=1/2$ and $|mo|=\sqrt3/2$ and hypotenuse $|vo|=1$, so its three barycentric coordinates have slopes $2$, $2/\sqrt3$ and $4/\sqrt3$; hence $L=4/\sqrt3$ and the uniform star radius of the star lemma is $\delta=1/(2L(D+1))=\sqrt3/24$ for $D=2$;

**(iv)** let $d_{\mathrm{gr}}$ be the graph distance of the hexagonal $1$-skeleton $C_6$ (the Cayley graph of the Coxeter group of type $A_2$, which is the dihedral group $D_3$ of order $6$, for its two standard generators, Davis Proposition 7.3.4). For a pair of vertices at graph distance $k\in\{1,2,3\}$ one has
$$d(v_0,v_k)=1,\ \sqrt3,\ 2\qquad(k=1,2,3),\qquad d_{\mathrm{gr}}(v_0,v_k)=1,\ 2,\ 3.$$
Thus $d$ and $d_{\mathrm{gr}}$ already disagree on vertices: $\sqrt3<2$ (the short diagonal is shorter than the two-edge boundary route) and $2<3$ (opposite vertices are joined by the straight segment through the centre, while the boundary arc has length $3$). The graph metric is therefore not the metric induced by the cell, and neither is the boundary arc length.
items.strategy: Enumerate the affine-inequality faces and bound the cell. A single convex cell gives chain distance equal to Euclidean distance by its one-step upper bound and the Euclidean triangle lower bound; straight segments prove geodesicity without Choice. Compute the twelve barycentric right triangles from coordinate inner products and base-height content: heights 1/2, sqrt(3)/4, sqrt(3)/2 give L=4/sqrt(3); lower-dimensional slopes are smaller and singleton slopes zero. D=2 gives delta=sqrt(3)/24. The two explicit reflection matrices are orthogonal involutions with order-three product; alternating words reduce to six distinct orbit points, giving the A2 presentation and orbit hull. Right-generator neighbors identify the Cayley six-cycle. Coordinates give squared distances 1,3,4 and modulo-six increments give graph distances 1,2,3.
items.proof_strategy: explicit hexagon coordinates, face enumeration, barycentric heights and content computation
